Thus, the powerliftcrs involved in this study experienced, in addition to the squat weight of 200kg, an 
clastic resistance of 150kg at the lowest position while sitting down on the box with knees at approximately ri

1. A greater mean and peak force were produced throughout the range of movement
2. The descent onto the box tended to be accelerated above the normal gravitational rate of 9.8m/sec squared, so
that greater eccentric force had to be generated to control the downward motion
3. The stronger eccentric loading and the brief transition period involved while sitting before exploding up
provided neuromuscular stimulation which approximates that usually encountered in popular plyom

4. The force generated during the later stages increased, in strong contrast to the situation of normal squatting in
which force production tends to decrease significantly.
As with the other combined method of free weights and isokinetics, it is important to note that there tend to be 
large individual variations and that the exact shape of the combined resistance curve depends on the magnitude of

Figure 7.13 Resisted box squatting under combined free weights and elastically resisted conditions.
Although this research was carried out on box squatting, similar combinations of free weights and elastic bands 
may be used very effectively over a variety of different ranges of movement with other major exercises such as the 
deadlift, the clean, the bench press, good mornings and one arm deadlifts. These bands may also be attached
414

########## PDF 426
SUPh'RTRAINJNG
between the fixed and moving parts of pulley and various other training machines, thereby offering combined free 
weights and band resistance for a wide variety of bodybuilding and general strength exercises.
Another hybrid training method involves the combined use of free weights and chains, a method that was also 
pioneered in the USA by Louie Simmons primarily for powerlifting purposes. In this case, heavy duty chains are 
attached at either end of the loaded barbell, so that, as the weight is lifted further off the floor, the more links of 
chain arc raised and the more the resistance increases. The additional resistance offered by the chains may be 
varied by using different gauges of chain or different combinations of heavy and lighter gauge chains.
Accelerated Powerm etrics
The use of elastic bands provides not only added resistance during the concentric phase of the movement, but it 
can also be allowed to accelerate the load during the eccentric phase, thereby providing involuntary or passive 
acceleration. We thus note that elastic bands and plyometric actions provide similar methods of enhancing muscic 
tension. In the case of plyometrics, the body or its limbs are subjected to greater force during the amortisation 
phase of the exercise by momentum acting on the body through the acceleration of gravity (e.g., during a drop 
jump) or the action of a propelled object, while in the case of band training, the greater force is provided by 
external elastic tension.
These methods of increasing force during the amortisation or eccentric phase of an exercise arc actually 
involuntary or passive, since muscle action is not being intentionally used to impose greater force on the body. 
There is, however, also an active or voluntary form of imposing greater force on the body, which may be called 
actively accelerated powermetrics.
Let me now elaborate on how one can use actively accelerated powermetrics to do the bench press, squat, dip 
for the jerk, ‘Romanian deadlift* (or mid range clean pull from the hang) and various other exercises in a way 
which can be even more forceful than the load dropping and catching methods discussed in Ch 4.2.3. This type 
of training may be done in two voluntary forms, namely accelerated eccentric and accelerated ballistic training, 
neither of which requires anyone or any special machine to drop the load onto your hands or feet such as the 
“plyometric bench'* described in Figure 4.6. As noted above, together with the passive acceleration imposed 
during the eccentric phase of an exercise by elastic bands, these methods can extend the repertoire of 
“powermetric” training drills. In summary, then, here are the four main ways of using accelerated powermetrics:
1. Passively accelerated eccentrics: Here bands are used, but, instead of resisting the action o f the stretched 
bands to decelerate the bar or keep it moving down at approximately constant speed during the ecccntric 
phase, allow the elastic tension to accelerate the bar during this phase. Then, after a suitable range of 
movement, halt the movement as rapidly as you can.
2. Passively accelerated eccentrics: Here you rely on a partner to accelerate the bar during the eccentric phase by 
pushing downwards on it, like an inverse form of “forced reps’*. Instead of resisting the action throughout the 
amortisation phase, allow the bar to accelerate and then, after a suitable range of movement, halt the movement 
as rapidly as you can.
3. Actively accelerated eccentrics: Here you rely solely on your muscles. Instead o f resisting the action of 
gravity to decelerate the bar or keep it moving down at approximately constant speed or allowing it to drop 
almost freely under gravitational acceleration during the ecccntric phase, you deliberately pull the bar 
downwards as fast as you can and stop the downward motion before you reach the end of the movement. For 
safety reasons, do not allow the accelerated load to force you into your extreme end position of joint action. 
Unlike the form of accelerated eccentrics offered by elastic bands, the force added to gravitational force ceases 
if one stops voluntarily accelerating the bar.
4. Actively accelerated ballistics (or rebounds): Here you again rely solely on your muscles. Instead of lowering 
the bar slowly or allowing it to drop under gravitational acceleration, deliberately pull the bar downwards as 
fast as you can, stop the downward motion at a suitable point before the end of the movement and as rapidly 
as you can, try to accelerate the bar upwards into a powerful concentric movement.
Whatever you do, do not overestimate your capabilities, because all of these forms of accelerated powermetrics 
can be very demanding on the body. In general, you should start learning this movement with relatively light 
loads in the bench press or squat (say, about 40-50kg, depending on your strength and training experience) and 
use very few repetitions. Obviously the load used in exercises which involve smaller and weaker muscic groups
415

########## PDF 427
SUPERTRAINING
should be considerably lower than that. Remember that this is really a type of'supramaximal' force training and it 
can impose extremely large stresses on your soft tissues.
The important thing to remember is that this form of training, according to Newton's Second Law, focuses on 
force being increased by means of acceleration and not added mass. As you progress, recall that maximal power 
production, depending on the specific exercise, occurs with loads of between 50-70 percent of one’s IRM, so it is 
unnecessary ever to exceed this range of loading in these accelerated training methods (unless one uses them over a 
very small range of motion).
7.4 Muscle Training
It is sometimes necessary to know which groups of muscles are carrying out a moving or stabilising role when an 
exercise programme is being devised. This analysis requires a good working knowledge of functional anatomy, 
especially as many terms used to describe popular movements in bodybuilding often disguise the intricacy and 
subtleties of the joint actions. For instance, 'bicep curls' do not involve the brachial biceps only, but also the 
brachialis and brachialis to differing degrees, depending on hand position and speed of movement.
It should be remembered that the concept of muscle isolation training which is rife in bodybuilding is very 
misleading, as discussed in detail earlier (4.2.9). Muscle isolation incorrectly implies that only one specific muscle 
group is activated by a given exercise. 
Isolation may occur to a significant extent when the resistance to 
movement is small, but with increasing load, the relevant stabilisers of the body and joints, as well as assistant 
movers, come more strongly into play.
This why it is vital to remember that all human movement involves the intricate orchestration of concurrent 
and sequential contractions of movers and stabilisers. 
Each muscular symphony is different for a specific 
sporting action and a knowledge of functional anatomy allows us to identify the muscle groups in each movement 
and how they are involved in conccntric, eccentric and isometric types of contraction. This section summarises 
some of the essential functional anatomy that was presented earlier in the form of Movement Matrices (see 3.7) to 
enable us to analyse joint actions in sport and to prescribe supplementary strengthening exercises on a 
kinesiologically logical basis.
Before any analysis of complex multi-articular movement is attempted, the last section at the end of Chapter 
3 (entitled Limitations o f Anatomical Movement Analysis) should be borne in mind. Here it was stressed that the 
classical methods of functional anatomy define a given muscle, for instance, as a flexor or extensor, on the basis of 
the torque that it produces around a single joint, but the nature of the body as a linked system of many joints 
means that muscles which do not span other joints can still produce acceleration about those joints.
Recently, largely as a consequence of individuals attempting to extrapolate to the general fitness world some 
of the muscle isolating methods used by physical therapists for injury rehabilitation, it has become fairly 
fashionable to encounter special programmes to train ‘core stabilisation’ with balancing tools such as wobble 
boards and physio balls, augmented by activation of the transversus abdominis (TA) to strengthen the trunk. All 
too often, it seems to be forgotten that stability of the core or trunk cannot be exhibited without the periphery of 
the body being firmly secured on a solid surface, unless, of course, the athlete has to use the core independently of 
the floor or any other apparatus, as in diving, trampolining and jumping. Well meaning instructions to activate 
TA during dynamic actions such as lifting and wrestling are highly inappropriate, because conscious intervention 
in any such movements can lead to “paralysis by analysis*’. Anyway, if the athlete is taught the optimal way to 
carry out any movement, the body naturally activates muscles in the most appropriate way for that given 
activity. After all, the body “knows only of movement, not muscles”. Finally, no research has yet shown that 
isolationist training or ball/board balancing skills transpose to ‘functional’ sporting action, so that time spent on 
such pursuits usually can be better spent on more sport specific drills, unless the aim is to resolve some injury.
7.4.1 A Summary of M ovem ents of the Join ts
As before, this section also approaches kinesiology from the point of view of joint actions rather than by analysis 
of which specific muscle groups produce a given movement. To use this information, simply identify the joint 
action and then identify which muscles produce that action. For a graphical method of obtaining the same 
information, consult the Movement Matrices in Section 3.7.

and scaleni).

Flexion: Mainly the hamstrings, assisted by sartorius, gracilis and gastrocnemius. Popliteus initiates flexion by 
unlocking the extended knee.
Medial rotation (of tibia relative to femur): Semimembranosus, semitendinosus, sartorius, gracilis, popliteus.
Lateral rotation (of tibia relative to femur): Biceps femoris.
Movements o f the Hip J o in t
Extension: Femoral biceps, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, hamstring portion of adductor magnus, gluteus 
maximus (when the action requires greater force).
Flexion: Iliopsoas, rectus femoris (particularly if the knee is extended), tensor fasciae latac, sartorius, adductor 
longus, adductor brevis, the adductor portion of adductor magnus, pectineus, the anterior fibres of gluteus mcdius 
and minimus.
Abduction: Gluteus medius and minimus, possibly weakly assisted by tensor fasciae latae, piriformis and 
obturator intemus.
Adduction: Adductor magnus, longus and brevis, assisted by gracilis and pectineus, with possible weak assistance 
from quadratus femoris and obturator extemus.
Medial rotation: Tensor fasciae latac, anterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus.
lateral rotation: Gluteus maximus, sartorius, iliopsoas, pcctineus, the posterior fibres of gluteus medius and 
minimus, the lateral rotators (piriformis, quadratus femoris, obturator intemus and extemus, gemellus superior 
and inferior).
Movements of the Shoulder Jo in t
Extension: Latissimus dorsi, teres major and minor, posterior deltoid, infraspinatus and the long head of triceps. 
Flexion: Across the chest - pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, coracobrachial is, biceps. Upwards in sagittal plane - 
posterior deltoid, upper trapezius (for scapular rotation).
Abduction: Deltoids, supraspinatus (for scapular rotation).
Adduction: Pcctoralis major, teres major, latissimus dorsi, coracobrachialis, subscapularis, and the long head of

########## PDF 429
SUPERTRAINING
Flexion: Brachialis, brachioradialis (particularly if the movement is rapid). Also biceps (if forearm is supinatcd) 
and pronator teres (if forearm is pronated).
Note: Apparent rotation of the elbow joint is actually rotation at the wrist - the radius and ulna twist about one another, so there is no 
rotation of the elbow joint as a whole.
M ovem ents of the Ankle J o in t
Plantarjlexion: Gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior and flexor digitorum longus, weakly assisted by plantaris, 
peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.
Dorsiflexion: Tibialis anterior, pcroneus tcrtius, extensor hallucis longus, and extensor digitorum longus.
Inversion: Flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior, assisted by extensor hallucis 
longus.
Evers ion: Extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius, peroneus longus, peroneus brevis.
7.4.2 Exam ination of Som e Joint Actions
The application of the Movement Matrices or the above summary enables us to appreciate how ill understood 
some popular exercises are. For instance, so-called 'calf raises' or 'heel raises' arc commonly regarded as exercises 
to develop gastrocnemius and soleus. However, it should be noted that plantarflexion also involves action of 
plantaris, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior. Moreover, inward rotation or 
inversion of the foot more strongly recruits the last three muscles named, so that heel raises with inversion tend to 
activate all of the plantarflexors more strongly. Popular emphasis on heel raising in invariably causes one to 
neglect the antagonistic action of the dorsiflexors such as tibialis anterior. The summary above reveals that it is 
important to dorsiflex with both inversion and eversion of the ankle if all dorsiflexors are to be exercised 
adequately.
It is important to distinguish between unilateral and bilateral actions of certain muscle groups, such as the 
erector spinae. Acting unilaterally, they serve to laterally extend the trunk, whereas acting bilaterally and 
symmetrically, they extend the trunk backwards without any lateral movement occurring. It should also be noted 
that lateral action of the long muscles of the back does not produce spinal rotation and that the only muscle of the 
back which is involved in spinal rotation is multifidus. The major initiators of trunk rotation are the internal and 
external obliques and the strengthening of these muscles, therefore, is vital for all sporting activities that require 
rotation of the trunk.
It should also be noted that rectus abdominis, although it might be considered an antagonist of the erector 
spinae, does not produce any lateral action of the trunk. Both groups of obliques acting bilaterally produce trunk 
flexion so as to augment action by rectus abdominis, so it is incorrect to state that trunk flexion is solely a result 
of contraction of rectus abdominis. It is also interesting to note that if situps are done with a lateral flexing of the 
trunk, the rectus abdominis are not significantly involved, but the obliques and psoas are strongly contracted.
7.5 Use of Strength Training Compendium
The classification and interrelation of the host of strength training means and methods is still at a stage similar to 
that of atomic physics earlier this century when no truly coherent scheme had been worked out to 
compartmentalise the rapidly growing list of sub-atomic particles. 
Relationships between different masses, 
charges, quantum numbers and spins of particles were intuitively suspected, but not theoretically formalised or 
experimentally confirmed.
Similarly, bodybuilding magazines and competitors in all aspects of the Iron Game identified a vast array of 
different training methods and techniques, while physiotherapists and other medical personnel separately 
developed their own scheme of physical conditioning, yet no overall grand scheme emerged to integrate the two 
approaches and their individual multitudes of training methods. Therefore, the author was invited to address the 
1989 conference of the NSCA (National Strength and Conditioning Association) in the USA to show how thera­
peutic PNF could serve as a complete conditioning system for the uninjured athlete and how it relates to existing 
strength training methods (Siff, 1989). Until that time, PNF was generally regarded as a special type of stretching 
system by sports coaches who used it. However, it was not appreciated that PNF can act as a training system 
for all aspects of musculoskeletal conditioning in the competitive athlete, nor did many physiotherapists know 
that some of the bodybuilding and weightlifting methods could be valuable in the rehabilitation setting.
418

########## PDF 430
SUPERTRAINING
An overview of this presentation and workshop acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above, which should 
enable the coach to select consult the list of principles and apply those procedures that best meet the needs of 
the athlete in a given situation. For instance, instead of prescribing the use of the pec-deck for conditioning the 
pectoral and deltoid muscles of a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, he would recommend the use of a pulley 
machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the 
body. The movement would be performed over a comfortable full range, involve multiple joints besides just the 
shoulder and position the joints to optimise strengthening (i.e. principles of 7.2.3.1).
The effectiveness of many other training activities in sport may similarly be enhanced by involving other 
PNF methods, such as pre-stretch, exercising of agonists and antagonists, use of static and dynamic conditions, 
cheating to compel stronger musclcs to help the weaker ones, optimal timing, use of full-range specific patterns of 
diagonal-spiral motions (details in Knott & Voss, 1977), application of maximal resistance throughout the non- 
ballistic movement range, and commencement of motion in the strongest range. Such PNF principles integrate 
very naturally into the extensive scheme of bodybuilding and weightlifting methods and thereby furnish an 
extremely comprehensive array of supplementary training variations which can be invaluable in all cross training 
programmes.
The neuromuscular emphasis of this integrated package of methods can be most helpful in enhancing the 
functional co-development of strength, flexibility, muscic endurance and speed in any particular movement. For 
instance, stretching exercises are often performed in a static manner separately from the main exercises, when their 
effectiveness would increase markedly if the latter were also to be used statically and dynamically over a full range 
with progressively increasing resistance incorporating relevant PNF procedures. Thus, the complementary nature 
of methods from the Iron Game and the field of rehabilitation may be seen to offer an impressive compendium of 
highly effective structural and functional training techniques. 
A thorough knowledge of these techniques is 
invaluable to the creative and dedicated coach.
7.6 Training for H ypertrophy?
There are numerous theories and beliefs about what the best formula is to follow for producing greatest muscle 
hypertrophy. One such concept is that every exercise must maintain a prolonged muscle tension time for at least 
40 seconds or so if one wishes to produce maximal hypertrophy.
Some have commented that “All the big bodybuilders who 1 trained with did their reps pretty fast, which 
makes me seriously question the Time Under Tension theory, though I am sure there are exceptions, as there always 
arc to each rule. However, it’s not the biggest guys I see who are counting the seconds on the way up or down. 
Others have added that “People with extreme genetics who are using huge amounts of drugs will probably get big no 
matter what kind of weight training and rep speed they’re doing. What's more important is finding out how much 
rep speed matters for a natural bodybuilder with average genetics."
Now, what we are all trying to identify here are the most important factors in stimulating muscle hypertrophy, 
or we should rather say, musculo-collagenous hypertrophy, since training affects the entire muscle complex, not just 
the muscles. 
Physical loading also stimulates bone hypertrophy, especially at the sites of maximal stress 
concentration, but that is of little consequence to the bodybuilder because bone size and definition are not seen by 
spectators, though this phenomenon may assist us later in answering some other questions about muscle growth. 
Any Hypertrophy Formula has to be based on many well-known observations on muscle physiology and 
mechanics. Some of these observations are:
1. The fundamental stimulus in all strength and tissue hypertrophy quite simply is physical loading.
2. The physical loading must not exceed the mechanical strength of the tissues involved.
3. Increase in strength and hypertrophy is not instantaneous, but occurs predominantly during a certain recovery 
period after loading
4. All tissues do not hypertrophy or strengthen at the same rate or to the same degree
5. Strength and hypertrophy increase is minimal unless a certain minimal threshold load is imposed
6. The minimal threshold is not fixed, but increases with level of adaptation, which ensures that rate of progress 
slows down or ceases
419

########## PDF 431
SUPERTRAINING
7. The concept of tension time per se is meaningless, since loading even for very prolonged periods may have no 
effects of strength and hypertrophy if the tension does not exceed this minimum threshold
8. The effects of tension on tissue depend not only on the magnitude or duration of the tension, but the way is 
which the tension is produced or maintained. 
For example, one can use high or low Rates of Tensioc 
Development, and one can increase tension by use of a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly 
accelerated load (in accordance with Newton II: Force = Mass x Acceleration)
9. Long periods of muscle 'time under tension' as imposed by cyclical activities such as endurance running, cycling 
and swimming are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy.
10. Continued increase in strength and hypertrophy is a consequence of progressive incremental increase in loading 
(principle of progressive overload)
11. Changes in strength and hypertrophy are not linear or continuous. For example, a 10% increase in load docs 
not necessarily produce a 10% increase in strength. Some changes may be delayed or marked at certain stages.
12. Muscles rarely arc able to produce 100% of their maximum potential, due to a variety of reasons such as 
protective inhibition by certain reflexes.
13. Increase in strength and hypertrophy may or may not be associated with some form of fatigue
14. It is difficult to distinguish between the limitations imposed by short-term fatigue and those imposed by reflex 
inhibition of maximal force production
15. Fatigue is not a single discrete factor, but a multi-faceted process involving phenomena such as central and 
peripheral fatigue, slow and fast fatigue, and short-term and long-term fatigue.
16. Muscle tension is not constant during any movement, but varies between zero and a certain maximum as joint 
angles change
17. Muscle tension is not produced under the same conditions throughout any movement, but changes between 
concentric, eccentric and isomctric modes of action
18. Musclcs comprise smaller groups of fibres which exhibit different rates of fatigue, fatiguc-resistance and ability 
to generate force (e.g. so-called slow and fast twitch fibres)
19. All muscle tension and patterns of muscle recruitment are a consequence of nervous activity, so that increase in 
strength and hypertrophy ultimately are the result of specific patterns of nervous excitation.
20. Increase in strength is not necessarily associated with increase in hypertrophy or vice versa
21. Strength and hypertrophy diminish if physical loading is not imposed regularly at certain intervals
22. Strength and hypertrophy increase may be stimulated by active muscle contraction, passive stretching, 
vibrational oscillation or external electrical stimulation.
There are many other observations which are relevant to our quest to find the ideal, individualised physique or 
strength building program, but these should suffice to show that a Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly 
prescriptive rule is oversimplistic in satisfying many of the above observations.
When someone stated that "People with extreme genetics who are using huge amounts o f drugs will probably 
get big no matter what kind of weight training and rep speed they're doing", he is probably far closer to the truth 
than anyone who religiously propounds simplistic Tension Time theories. 
One has to remember that the 
marketability of a certain fitness figure or group, according to well-established marketing principles, depends on 
slogans and simply stated formulae.
The public usually feels far more comfortable with cerebrally undemanding mantras and 'fast food' solutions 
than with far more accurate, more complex methods. That is a major reason why many fitness figures write as they 
do and market their catch phrases simplistically as they do - society has been processed by the mass media to 
behave like that and they usually do not want to be forced to think too deeply or to have their convenient current 
beliefs questioned, because that entails a serious threat to their psychological safety. Humankind has always been 
like that and they receive what they have been processed or educated to want.
420

########## PDF 432
SUPERTRAINING
DESIGNING SPORT SPECIFIC 
STRENGTH PROGRAMMES
Preparation for sport comprises two distinct conditioning aspects: training and practice. These aspects are often 
confused, which frequently results in conditioning sessions being structured to provide both training and practice, 
a compromise which generally does not produce optimal results.
Training refers to the process of enhancing the physical and mental condition of the athlete, whereas practice 
refers to the process of perfecting the technical skills demanded by the particular sport. Traditionally, 'practice' 
in the West in many sports has included elements o f ’fitness' training in the form of jogging around the field, 
push-ups, sit-ups and other military type activities before game practice. This, however, wastes a coach's 
expertise and time. Ideally, the role of a coach is to cnhance game skills, with the fitness conditioning handled by 
specific conditioning coaches, as is rapidly becoming the case with the more popular sports in the USA.
In identifying the distinction between training and practice, one must remember that training for a specific 
sport may be either beneficial or detrimental to performance and that practice may suffer as a result of 
inappropriate conditioning. This is becoming increasingly likely, since 'cross training' has increased in popularity 
among fitness instructors with little experience in its use, which has led to scientifically dubious combinations of 
cycling, circuit training, jogging, swimming and so forth being imposed on athletes. Resurgence in the popularity 
of circuit training in commercial gymnasia is also exacerbating the problem. It is apparent that the principles of 
sport specific strength training need to become better known, particularly in the West.
Arduous fitness training regimes in the gymnasium or on the sports field may not necessarily result in 
superior competitive ability. Conversely, avoidance of supplementary training may prevent an athlete from 
fulfilling his or her potential. All supplementary activities and recuperation methods must be carefully selected, 
planned and sequenced to ensure that they contribute directly to enhancing sports performance. One even has to 
pose the question whether or not the time spent on a particular supplementary activity could not be better spent 
on sport specific practice.
8.1 Prelim inary C onsiderations
Among the most important factors for introducing scicntific sport specific training are :
1. Sports training must be a year-round and multi-year process. An off-season lay-off followed by less than 
one month of moderate pre-season training can be a major cause of low levels of overall fitness among 
athletes and an increased incidence o f injuries. The early off-season is one period where popular cross 
training can be used successfully. Generally, the integration of supplementary or cross training becomes 
increasingly difficult as the season progresses and player fitness or proficiency improves.
2. Specialist coaches are required for the different components of sports conditioning. Very few single coaches 
are equipped to handle strategic skills, movement skills, physical conditioning, psychological preparation, 
biomechanical analysis, fitness assessment and rehabilitation routines. Just as there is a playing team, so 
there has to be an efficient coaching team comprising all the relevant experts.
3. Scientific fitness training has to be integrated into every athlete's programme. In particular, it is not possible 
to enhance adequately strength, hypertrophy, speed and flexibility without use of supplementary resistance 
training. This type of training is most efficiently achieved in an appropriately equipped gymnasium using 
logically selected exercises sequenced carefully in terms of intensity, volume, muscic group, patterns of 
movement and restoration intervals.
Because few gymnasium staff have formal training in designing scientific supplementary conditioning 
routines, athletes should be provided with scientific programmes prepared by teams of experts and 
supervised by accredited sports conditioning coaches. Ideally, every major sports complex should have its 
own conditioning gymnasium to ccntralise all aspects of in-season and off-season preparation for players.
421

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

lines: - Fig 6.40, read by eye: block 1 over about months 2-4 (taller), block 2 over about months 6-7 (shorter); phases I about months 1-4, II about month 5, III about months 6-8, IV about months 9-11. For a large mesocycle (Fig 6.46, PDF pp. 399-400), aerobic training "covers the first half of the large mesocycle during which the GPP and concentrated strength loading take place," then speed, then specialised endurance, with competitions as a main way to develop it.
**Long-duration endurance (monocyclic, Fig 6.41).**

-- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396).

+- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396). The authors' reason for the long preparation: "with reference to the predominance of low intensity work (relative to other groups of sports), the optimal date for increasing the current adaptation reserves is deferred, a detail which is taken into account in the model" (PDF p. 396, checked against the page image).

# Inertial (Flywheel) and Elastic Resistance: Different Force Profiles From Free Weights, Each With Its Own Limitation

**What it is** — The authors note that specialised equipment for training against a load's
inertia (rather than its weight) is rarely used, despite the concept warranting more serious
attention. Two solutions are given: applying force against a horizontal wheel or a
suspended, pendulum-like load, or spinning a heavy flywheel ergometer with the arms or legs
(Fig 4.4, elbow-flexion flywheel device, Verkhoshansky 1977). "In the first example, one can
vary the amount of weight and in the second, the moment of inertia of the flywheel to affect
speed of contraction." Flywheel ergometers can be used several ways: "accelerating against
high inertia, using the heavy wheel to compel one to operate at a certain cadence, and
opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to decelerate the wheel", with
these methods combinable in short or mixed bursts. Elastic bands are treated as a separate
case: resistance follows Hooke's Law (F = kx, where k is the spring constant and x is
extension), so elastic force "begins from zero value and increases with movement range";
therefore, the authors state, "elastic materials should not be used for developing
starting-strength in ballistic movements or for developing explosive-strength". Inference:
those qualities need force available from the very start of the movement, which elastics
cannot supply. For strength-endurance over a selected range, however, an elastic band's
length and elasticity can be chosen so its resistance changes minimally over the working
range, a method "sometimes used by swimmers" to develop pulling strength-endurance (Fig 4.5,
Verkhoshansky 1977). Resistance at "sticking points" can be reduced by moving toward the
band's attachment point, or increased by moving away from it; resistance can also be varied
across the full range by accelerating free weights through a decreasing-resistance portion
of the lift (so-called Compensatory Acceleration Training, see
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]) or by using dedicated variable-resistance
machines. (PDF p. 230, printed p. 219, "4.2.2 Resistance and Strength Training," Figs
4.4-4.5.)

**Why it works** — For inertial devices, the authors' reasoning is that force against a
load's inertia (F = ma) rather than its weight (F = m(g+a)): "Under conditions where
strength is directed against the inertia of the load, predominantly the speed of muscular
contraction is stimulated" (PDF p. 229, printed p. 218), so that in the inertia case "it
is easy to appreciate the possibility for overcoming the opposing tendency between the
weight of the load and the speed of muscular contraction" (p.219). Inference: the athlete
trains speed of contraction against a resistance that is not present at rest and appears
only once acceleration is applied. For elastic bands, the mechanism is Hooke's Law itself:
resistance is proportional to extension, so it begins from zero at the start of the range
and increases with range (p.219). Inference: this is the opposite loading curve from what
ballistic and explosive-strength work needs.

**When to apply** — Inference: use flywheel or inertial devices when the training goal is
speed of muscular contraction against inertia specifically (per
[[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]]), varying the moment of
inertia (flywheel) or the amount of weight (pendulum or horizontal wheel) to adjust the
demand, and consider "opposing the angular momentum via eccentric muscle action to
decelerate the wheel" (p.219) as a separate use of the same device. Use elastic bands specifically for strength-endurance work over a selected range
(the authors' cited example: swimmers' pulling strength-endurance), choosing band length and
elasticity to minimise resistance variation across that range, and use position along the
band (closer to or farther from the attachment) to manage sticking-point loading.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use elastic-band resistance for developing
starting-strength or explosive-strength in ballistic movements; the authors state this
directly, because elastic resistance "begins from zero value and increases with movement
range" (p.219). Inference: the flywheel and pendulum devices described are purpose-built
apparatus, which the authors say is "rarely used in training" (p.219) (a 1992 University of the Witwatersrand student
biomechanics project supplied the plyometric bench-press device shown nearby, Fig 4.6, PDF
p. 231, printed p. 220, a related but separate kinetic-energy device); the authors give no standardised commercial
specification for the flywheel or pendulum devices described here.

**Example** — Inference: a swim coach building pulling strength-endurance with resistance
bands, per the authors' own cited example, should select a band whose resistance changes
little across the stroke's working range, rather than a stiffer band whose resistance would
spike sharply near full extension; a sprint or jump coach chasing starting-strength or
explosive-strength should not substitute elastic-band resistance for free weights or
inertial-device training for that specific quality.

**Related** — [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]],
[[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]].

# Rhea et al. 2009 — Squat speed, bands, and lower-body power

> **Citation**
> Rhea, M. R., Kenn, J. G., & Dermody, B. M. (2009). Alterations in speed of squat movement and the use of accommodated resistance among college athletes training for power. *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 23*(9). https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b3e1b6

## Why it was promoted

This intervention compares slow squatting, fast squatting, and fast squatting with elastic-band accommodating resistance in collegiate athletes.

## Research question

Do squat movement speed and accommodating resistance differentially affect jump power and squat strength?

## Population and context

- Forty-eight male NCAA Division I baseball, track, football, and basketball athletes.
- Sixteen athletes per group.
- All had prior resistance and plyometric experience.

## Study design and methods

- Twelve-week randomized group intervention after three weeks of familiarization.
- Groups used slow squats, fast squats, or fast squats plus elastic bands.
- Other lower-body resistance, sprint, and plyometric programming was similar.

## Key findings

- Jump power improved 17.8% in the fast-plus-bands group, 11.0% with fast squats, and 4.8% with slow squats. [p. 4]
- Fast-plus-bands exceeded slow training for power improvement (p = .02); its difference from fast-only did not reach .05 (p = .09). [p. 5]
- Squat-strength changes did not differ significantly among groups. [p. 5]
- Fast-plus-bands and slow training had similar descriptive strength gains, about 9.4–9.6%. [p. 5]

## Limitations and applicability

- Statistical power averaged only .67. [p. 4]
- The intervention combined several training modes, though squat condition was the intended group difference.
- Only male collegiate athletes were included.
- Band tension and bar-speed prescriptions require equipment-specific replication.

## Practitioner interpretation

Intent and velocity matter for power development, but the study does not prove bands are superior to every fast-load strategy. Use bands when they help preserve acceleration through the range and verify bar-speed and jump response.

# Frost et al. 2010 — Biomechanical evaluation of resistance modes

> **Citation**
> Frost, D. M., Cronin, J., & Newton, R. U. (2010). A biomechanical evaluation of resistance: Fundamental concepts for training and sports performance. *Sports Medicine, 40*(4), 303-326. https://doi.org/10.2165/11319420-000000000-00000

## Why it was promoted

This review provides a mechanical framework for understanding why constant, ballistic, accommodating, and variable resistance produce different force, velocity, power, and muscle-activity profiles.

## Research question

How do the mechanical properties of resistance modes constrain movement kinetics and kinematics, and what does that imply for strength and power training?

## Population and context

- Narrative review of resistance-training biomechanics rather than a new participant study.
- Covers constant free-weight resistance, stretch-shortening-cycle actions, ballistic movements, hydraulic and isokinetic devices, cams and levers, bands and chains, and pneumatic resistance.
- The applied context is transfer from gym-based strength and power work to sport performance.

## Study design and methods

- Conceptual and narrative synthesis organized around Newtonian mechanics and published acute studies.
- Compares resistance modes through load inertia, acceleration, force, impulse, velocity, power, range of motion, and muscle activity.
- No systematic-search, risk-of-bias, or pooled-effect method is reported.

## Key findings

- With 45% 1RM, projecting the load in a ballistic action increased mean velocity by 27.3%, extended acceleration through 96% rather than 60% of displacement, and increased peak velocity by 36.5% in the cited comparison. [p. 12]
- In the same cited work, ballistic execution increased mean force by 35% but did not increase peak acceleration, peak force, time to peak force, or rate of force development. [p. 12]
- The review concludes that constant resistance creates substantial phase-dependent variation in kinetics and kinematics, while ballistic execution reduces deceleration constraints but does not solve every power-development limitation. [p. 21]
- Bands may sustain acceleration and late-phase force or velocity, but the review states that improved transfer to sport had not been demonstrated and much acute evidence showed no difference from load-matched free weights. [p. 21]
- Pneumatic resistance has plausible mechanical advantages through lower moving mass, but the hypothesized benefit for sport-specific velocity and power remained untested. [p. 21]

## Limitations and applicability

- This is a narrative biomechanical review using heterogeneous exercises, devices, populations, loads, and outcome definitions.
- Acute mechanical advantages do not necessarily produce superior chronic adaptation or sport performance.
- Several proposed benefits of bands and pneumatic resistance were theoretical or unsupported by direct transfer studies at publication.
- Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): a resistance device cannot be selected from its label alone; exercise, load, intent, range, and athlete status determine the actual stimulus.

# Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 — Regression model for load at maximum power

> **Citation**
> Jandacka, D., & Vaverka, F. (2008). A regression model to determine load for maximum power output. *Sports Biomechanics, 7*(3), 361–371. https://doi.org/10.1080/14763140802266934

## Why it was promoted

The study shows that the load associated with maximum measured power depends on exercise, sex, and whether power is calculated over the acceleration phase or the full upward movement.

## Research question

Can nonlinear regression describe the load-power relationship in bench press and countermovement squat and identify the external load associated with maximum power output?

## Population and context

- Fifty-five male and 48 female physical-education students.
- Men averaged 21.8 ± 1.5 years and women 21.1 ± 1.2 years.
- Participants were healthy, but were not described as trained power athletes.
- Testing used Smith-machine bench press and countermovement squat.

## Study design and methods

- Laboratory modeling study completed across four sessions.
- Participants completed familiarization, 1RM testing, and power testing at systematically increasing loads.
- Loads were tested at 0, 10, 30, 50, 70, 90, and 100% 1RM with maximal intended velocity.
- Force, velocity, acceleration, and power were used in nonlinear regression models for the acceleration phase and complete upward movement.

## Key findings

- For the acceleration phase, estimated optimal bench-press loads were 56 ± 9% 1RM in men and 63 ± 8% 1RM in women. [p. 11]
- Corresponding countermovement-squat loads were 47 ± 9% of maximum dynamic strength in men and 54 ± 9% in women. [p. 11]
- Significant sex and exercise effects indicated that a single universal percentage could not represent every task or group. [p. 11]
- The authors recommended linking load to the measured force-velocity-power relationship rather than relying only on 1RM percentage. [p. 11]

## Limitations and applicability

- The sample comprised young physical-education students rather than sport-specific elite athletes.
- Results depended on Smith-machine technique, the device and calculation method, and the distinction between acceleration-phase and full-movement power.
- The regression equations were developed and evaluated in the same cohort; independent predictive validation was not reported.
- Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): group mean percentages are starting estimates, not individualized optimal-load prescriptions or evidence of superior training adaptation.

## Practitioner interpretation

# Rhea et al. 2009 — Squat speed, bands, and lower-body power

> **Citation**
> Rhea, M. R., Kenn, J. G., & Dermody, B. M. (2009). Alterations in speed of squat movement and the use of accommodated resistance among college athletes training for power. *Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 23*(9). https://doi.org/10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b3e1b6

## Why it was promoted

This intervention compares slow squatting, fast squatting, and fast squatting with elastic-band accommodating resistance in collegiate athletes.

## Research question

Do squat movement speed and accommodating resistance differentially affect jump power and squat strength?

## Population and context

- Forty-eight male NCAA Division I baseball, track, football, and basketball athletes.
- Sixteen athletes per group.
- All had prior resistance and plyometric experience.

## Study design and methods

- Twelve-week randomized group intervention after three weeks of familiarization.
- Groups used slow squats, fast squats, or fast squats plus elastic bands.
- Other lower-body resistance, sprint, and plyometric programming was similar.

## Key findings

- Jump power improved 17.8% in the fast-plus-bands group, 11.0% with fast squats, and 4.8% with slow squats. [p. 4]
- Fast-plus-bands exceeded slow training for power improvement (p = .02); its difference from fast-only did not reach .05 (p = .09). [p. 5]
- Squat-strength changes did not differ significantly among groups. [p. 5]
- Fast-plus-bands and slow training had similar descriptive strength gains, about 9.4–9.6%. [p. 5]

## Limitations and applicability

- Statistical power averaged only .67. [p. 4]
- The intervention combined several training modes, though squat condition was the intended group difference.
- Only male collegiate athletes were included.
- Band tension and bar-speed prescriptions require equipment-specific replication.

## Practitioner interpretation

Intent and velocity matter for power development, but the study does not prove bands are superior to every fast-load strategy. Use bands when they help preserve acceleration through the range and verify bar-speed and jump response.

# Frost et al. 2010 — Biomechanical evaluation of resistance modes

> **Citation**
> Frost, D. M., Cronin, J., & Newton, R. U. (2010). A biomechanical evaluation of resistance: Fundamental concepts for training and sports performance. *Sports Medicine, 40*(4), 303-326. https://doi.org/10.2165/11319420-000000000-00000

## Why it was promoted

This review provides a mechanical framework for understanding why constant, ballistic, accommodating, and variable resistance produce different force, velocity, power, and muscle-activity profiles.

## Research question

How do the mechanical properties of resistance modes constrain movement kinetics and kinematics, and what does that imply for strength and power training?

## Population and context

- Narrative review of resistance-training biomechanics rather than a new participant study.
- Covers constant free-weight resistance, stretch-shortening-cycle actions, ballistic movements, hydraulic and isokinetic devices, cams and levers, bands and chains, and pneumatic resistance.
- The applied context is transfer from gym-based strength and power work to sport performance.

## Study design and methods

- Conceptual and narrative synthesis organized around Newtonian mechanics and published acute studies.
- Compares resistance modes through load inertia, acceleration, force, impulse, velocity, power, range of motion, and muscle activity.
- No systematic-search, risk-of-bias, or pooled-effect method is reported.

## Key findings

- With 45% 1RM, projecting the load in a ballistic action increased mean velocity by 27.3%, extended acceleration through 96% rather than 60% of displacement, and increased peak velocity by 36.5% in the cited comparison. [p. 12]
- In the same cited work, ballistic execution increased mean force by 35% but did not increase peak acceleration, peak force, time to peak force, or rate of force development. [p. 12]
- The review concludes that constant resistance creates substantial phase-dependent variation in kinetics and kinematics, while ballistic execution reduces deceleration constraints but does not solve every power-development limitation. [p. 21]
- Bands may sustain acceleration and late-phase force or velocity, but the review states that improved transfer to sport had not been demonstrated and much acute evidence showed no difference from load-matched free weights. [p. 21]
- Pneumatic resistance has plausible mechanical advantages through lower moving mass, but the hypothesized benefit for sport-specific velocity and power remained untested. [p. 21]

## Limitations and applicability

- This is a narrative biomechanical review using heterogeneous exercises, devices, populations, loads, and outcome definitions.
- Acute mechanical advantages do not necessarily produce superior chronic adaptation or sport performance.
- Several proposed benefits of bands and pneumatic resistance were theoretical or unsupported by direct transfer studies at publication.
- Additional transfer limitation (practitioner interpretation): a resistance device cannot be selected from its label alone; exercise, load, intent, range, and athlete status determine the actual stimulus.

## Practitioner interpretation

# Choose Supplementary Sports by the Fitness Qualities They Build and the Phase They Serve, Not by the Sport's Label

**What it is** — The authors define Western "cross training" as "using relevant secondary sports to augment the training effect produced in an athlete's primary sport," and tie it to the two ways of combining training from 5.3: supplementary activities can be prescribed "concurrently with the athlete's main sport on the same day or during the same training phase or in a definite sequence where one supplementary activity gives way to another and finally to the main sport over a given period" (PDF p. 309 / printed p. 298). In Russia and Eastern Europe, they write, the choice "does not simply focus primarily on the type of sport used, but rather on the relationship between the motor and fitness qualities in the supplementary activities and the primary sport," with "qualitative and quantitative modelling of each sport involved so as to ensure that the supplementary sports do not impair performance in the primary sport." Their example of the wrong approach: "It is inadequate, for example, to state that track-and-field athletics, rugby or American football require the development of strength, so that heavy weight training must constitute appropriate cross training ... this simplistic approach can offer little more than short term progress" (PDF p. 309 / printed p. 298). **What it is** — The strength an athlete can generate depends on body posture. The plot of
the external force (or moment of force) against a measure of body position, such as joint
angle, is a **strength curve** (printed p. 39). In single joints, strength curves take three
general forms: ascending, descending and concave (figure 2.21, after Hay & Komi 1992,
printed p. 40). Figure 2.22 (Zatsiorsky & Raitsin 1973, average data of 24 athletes, printed
p. 41): elbow flexion Fmm is reached at 90°, with strength about 46% of Fmm at 0° and about
50% at 150°; shoulder flexion is strongest with the arm slightly behind the trunk (−30°,
100%) and falls to about 37% at 150° (percentages read from the figure). The weakest
positions are the **sticking points**: "The heaviest weight that is lifted through a full
range of joint motion cannot be greater than the strength at the weakest point" (printed p.
41). Fmm results from muscular forces that undergo two transformations: muscle-tendon forces
→ joint moments → strength (end-point force) (printed pp. 41-42). Muscle tension depends on
muscle length for two reasons: the overlap of actin and myosin filaments (cross-bridge
number) and the contribution of elastic forces, especially from parallel elastic
components. As a general rule, with a few exceptions (for example, the rectus femoris in
some bicyclists), muscles exert smaller tension at smaller lengths and higher forces when
stretched (printed p. 42). As a joint nears the limit of its range, passive elastic forces
rise: in arm cocking in pitching, external rotation of the shoulder approaches 180°, and the
deformed muscles and soft tissues "contribute to the joint torques that reach maximal
values" (printed p. 42, figure 2.23, after Fleisig et al. 1995: 64 N·m and 67 N·m, 310 N,
with the arm drawn at 165°). For two-joint muscles, Fmm depends on the position of both
joints: with the knee maximally flexed and the ankle plantarflexed, the gastrocnemius cannot
produce active force, "a leg position [that] can be used for selective training of the
soleus muscle" (printed p. 42). Joint moment = muscle tension × muscle moment arm (M = Fd).
The moment arm of the biceps brachii (long head) was 11.5 mm at 180° (full extension) and
45.5 mm at 90° of elbow flexion; with equal tension, the moment and the external force would
change fourfold (printed pp. 42-43). The joint strength curve is the product of the muscle
tension-angle curve and the moment arm-angle curve (figure 2.24, printed p. 43). (PDF pp.
48-53, printed pp. 39-44.)

----
**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force: that is,
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg, roughly two-thirds of their maximum**,
producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at maximal load,
and time to execute the lift "increases by 282%" (the text does not state the reference
point this percentage is measured from). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The
Effect of the Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

content.content:
chapter: "3.5.3"
# Two Reflex Phenomena With Direct Stretching Applications: The Positive Supportive Reaction and Voluntary Relaxation
**What it is** — Two specific, named reflex phenomena the authors connect directly to
stretching practice. First, the positive supportive reaction (Guyton, 1984): any form of
stretching that exerts pressure on the soles of the feet or palms of the hands produces
strong reflex extension of the limb concerned, stiffening and stabilizing it against
external pressure (including body/trunk weight). The authors state this makes toe-touching
stretches in standing versus seated positions neuromuscularly different procedures,
because the locus of pressure on the sole or palm determines the position to which the
limb will extend, a mechanism physiotherapists use in PNF to guide a patient into a
specific pattern. Second, electromyographic (EMG) silence can persist in muscles being
passively stretched, regardless of stretch speed, meaning subjects can consciously relax a
muscle below the tension normal stretch reflexes would otherwise produce (Basmajian, 1978);
the authors infer from this that voluntary mental control or biofeedback techniques can
play a useful role in stretching and flexibility procedures. (PDF pp. 188-190, printed pp.
177-179.)
chapter: "1.16"
# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)
**What it is** — A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality, an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
speed-strength endurance, strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength,
flexibility-endurance, flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill,
speed-skill, and skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass)
matter separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF
chapter: "3.5.9"
# Ten Ways Coaches Can Train an Athlete's Ability to Relax Muscles on Demand
**What it is** — Following the claim that spurious muscle tension, not just tissue
stiffness, can limit functional ROM (see
[[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]]), the
authors list methods for improving the ability to relax muscles: (1) contract-relax,
hold-relax, and other PNF methods using stretch reflexes to promote relaxation; (2) sudden
unloading, the abrupt removal of external resistance under strong isometric or dynamic
conditions (e.g. the end of a jerk, completion of a heavy squat/bench press, releasing a
thrown shot or medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction), reported
as producing the greatest relaxation response of all listed means, and becoming more
effective the more closely the contraction-relaxation process is tied to the actual
sporting action; (3) changing muscle groups from tension to relaxation in a controlled,
gradual manner or through a series of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation
method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles

lines: **When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.

-**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin on the remedy and on the beginners limit, not on the critique (the basis for the `contested` rating).** Issurin agrees that traditional complex training falls short for elite athletes: the library's brief of Issurin 2016 says the review "repeats the book's critique of traditional planning" ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). He contests the remedy: his multi-targeted blocks train a minimal number of targets, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]). He also contests who the concentrated approach is for: the brief records "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads (brief, p. 11), against the book's view that complex loading is "applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380). The brief reports 28 studies supporting the multi-targeted model, but they are Issurin's own non-systematic, author-curated selection, with varied designs, populations, outcomes and comparators (brief, p. 11), not a pooled estimate. Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.

+**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin on the remedy and on the beginners limit, not on the critique (the basis for the `contested` rating).** Issurin agrees that traditional complex training falls short for elite athletes: the library's brief of Issurin 2016 says the review "repeats the book's critique of traditional planning," where "the book" is Issurin's own Block Periodization ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inference: traditional planning there means developing many abilities at once, the same complex organisation this entry's authors criticise. He contests the remedy: his multi-targeted blocks train a minimal number of targets, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]). He also contests who the concentrated approach is for: the brief records "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads (brief, p. 11), against the book's view that complex loading is "applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380). The brief reports 28 studies supporting the multi-targeted model, but they are Issurin's own non-systematic, author-curated selection, with varied designs, populations, outcomes and comparators (brief, p. 11), not a pooled estimate. So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.

**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).

# PNF Is a Whole Conditioning System Built on Five P-Factors, Not Just a Stretching Method

**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: he states that an overview of his 1989 NSCA presentation and workshop (Siff, 1989) "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Grouped here (the grouping is mine; the items are his): movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.

**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).

**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). His own scope claim: PNF can improve "all the S-factors of fitness ... except cardiovascular endurance and psychological fitness" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405; see [[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]]). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.

**When NOT to apply** — Siff's case that PNF is a complete athletic conditioning system is argued, not tested: he gives no training study, and "No training method could be required to offer much more than this repertoire to qualify as an all-round conditioning system" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405) is a judgment. The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Two source oddities: the principles say "Use of distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (principle 18) while the developmental list gives "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405); and procedure 4 attributes the stretch reflex in the lengthened range to "Starling's Law" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

**Example** — Siff's own: for a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "he would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").

**Related** — [[framework--pnf-activation-and-relaxation-techniques]], [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]], [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]] (the reflexes PNF uses, Fig 3.33), [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (the overflow principle), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (PNF as a stretching category, 3.5.8), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (PNF use of the positive supportive reaction)
