# PNF Is a Whole Conditioning System Built on Five P-Factors, Not Just a Stretching Method

**What it is** — Section 7.2 is Siff's: he states that an overview of his 1989 NSCA presentation and workshop (Siff, 1989) "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2 above" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). He writes that coaches regard PNF (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation) as "a special type of sophisticated stretching," but "it is actually an entire system of therapy comprising a broad spectrum of different techniques and procedures," of which stretching is "but one of many aspects" (PDF p. 414 / printed p. 403). History: PNF "was developed by Herman Kabat from 1946-1951" on work by Sherrington, Hellebrand, McGraw and Pavlov (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Definition: "a system for promoting the response of neuromuscular mechanisms by stimulating the proprioceptors"; Knott and Voss say its techniques involve "placing a demand where a response is required," which Siff ties to the SAID principle (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Two types: classical PNF, "the hands-on clinical approach described in the Knott and Voss text," and modified PNF, which "adapts certain PNF techniques and principles for application by hand or apparatus in physical conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). The structure is "five P-factors: Principles, Procedures, Patterns, Positions and Postures, with joint Pivots and Pacing (Timing) as important sub-categories" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Siff lists 23 principles (PDF pp. 416-417 / printed pp. 405-406). Grouped here (the grouping is mine; the items are his): movement form (spiral and diagonal patterns; motion crossing the sagittal midline; all movement components, flexion-extension, adduction-abduction, internal-external rotation; multiple joint and muscle action; comfortable full range; appropriate joint positioning); loading (maximal resistance through the range of non-ballistic movement; maximal resistance to promote "overflow (irradiation) of muscle activity from stronger to weaker patterns"; commencement of motion in the strongest range; stronger muscles augmenting the weaker; "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort"); neural (judicious eliciting of reflexes; sensory cues; visuo-motor and audio-motor coordination; agonists and antagonists; static and dynamic conditions; repeated contractions for motor learning); progression (primitive to complex; each phase laying foundations for the next; all activities integrated and goal directed); and adjuncts (cold, electrostimulation, massage, vibration, stroking). Positions and postures hold some joints stable so "All action can then take place around specific joints as pivots"; pacing ("normal timing") is "the timing of the phases of a movement or series of movements which occur naturally in an uninjured, healthy person" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Quotes from PDF pp. 414-418 are from the text layer.

**Why it works** — Siff's rationale is that "all physical conditioning depends primarily on neuromuscular processes involving sensitive receptors (proprioceptors) in the muscles, tendons and joints," so "Appropriate recruitment of the various stretch reflexes of the body ... forms a vital part of PNF conditioning" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Muscle contraction "is really the end-product of the interaction of various voluntary and reflex neuromotor processes," and bodybuilding-style training "over-emphasizes the role of muscle contraction" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). He names the reflexes used: the phasic and tonic components of the myotatic stretch reflex (short and long duration stretching loads give different responses), the Golgi tendon reflex to "reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and reciprocal inhibition, which "can produce a significantly stronger contraction of the agonists" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404). Maximal contraction through the range ensures "summation," the adding of motor-unit twitches by more units or a higher firing rate (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404).

**When to apply** — Use the 23 principles as a checklist when designing or reviewing supplementary exercises: Siff says "employment of any of the above principles in training implies conscious or unconscious reliance on aspects of the PNF system" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). His own scope claim: PNF can improve "all the S-factors of fitness ... except cardiovascular endurance and psychological fitness" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405; see [[framework--s-factors-pyramidal-fitness-model]]). Positions as pivots matter in ordinary lifts: a dumbbell curl "with the elbow dug firmly into the side" produces "activation patterns and results which are distinctly different" from one with elbow and shoulder free, and the unrestrained curl adds cheating, trapezius involvement and "downward traction ... at the shoulder joint" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the PNF principles fit best in that small assistance share and in Athletic Medicine handoffs, where multi-joint diagonal patterns can replace single-joint machine work.

**When NOT to apply** — Siff's case that PNF is a complete athletic conditioning system is argued, not tested: he gives no training study, and "No training method could be required to offer much more than this repertoire to qualify as an all-round conditioning system" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405) is a judgment. The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Two source oddities: the principles say "Use of distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (principle 18) while the developmental list gives "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405); and procedure 4 attributes the stretch reflex in the lengthened range to "Starling's Law" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

**Example** — Siff's own: for a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "he would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). # PNF Procedures: Three Activation Techniques, Three Antagonist Reversals and Three Relaxation (Stretching) Techniques

**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) lists nine PNF procedures: manual contacts to guide movement; "maximal tolerated resistance"; oral commands and non-verbal cues; maximal stretch reflex in the lengthened range; timing and sequencing; "traction or approximation (compression) to stimulate joint receptors"; "recuperative motion to reduce or avoid fatigue produced by resisted activity"; Specific Activation Techniques; and Specific Relaxation Techniques (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406, text layer). He expands the last two (PDF pp. 417-418 / printed pp. 406-407, text layer):

- Activation. Repeated Contractions (RC): "precise sequences or patterns of isometric, concentric and eccentric contraction, sometimes augmented by eliciting various neuromuscular reflexes (i.e. methods which may be similar to some types of plyometrics)." Rhythmic Initiation (RI): voluntary relaxation, passive movement and repeated dynamic contractions, "valuable with subjects who struggle to initiate activity because of rigidity or spasticity." Reversal of Antagonists (RA), in three forms: slow reversal (dynamic antagonist contraction, then dynamic agonist contraction); slow reversal-hold (dynamic then isometric contraction of the antagonist, then the same for the agonist); rhythmic stabilisation (isometric antagonist then isometric agonist, "thereby producing co-contraction").
- Relaxation (the techniques coaches call PNF stretching). Contract-Relax (CR): "a dynamic contraction of the antagonist against maximal resistance, followed by a phase of relaxation," repeated from the limit of pain-free range; the practitioner resists "as strongly as possible," tells the client to relax, waits for relaxation, then moves the limb passively "to its new limit of extension" for "a few repetitions." Hold-Relax (HR): the same "except that isometric rather than dynamic contraction against maximal resistance is applied." Slow-Reversal-Hold-Relax (SRHR): "dynamic contraction of the antagonists involved, isometric contraction of the antagonists, brief voluntary relaxation, and finally, dynamic contraction of the agonists," over several repetitions "to enhance functional flexibility."

**Why it works** — For reversals, Siff's reason is functional: antagonist reversal "occurs naturally in numerous activities such as walking, running and sawing wood," and "If the antagonists do not reverse competently in terms of strength, speed and coordination, motor efficiency is impaired" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For RC: "Repetition of muscle contraction is necessary for motor learning and the development of strength, muscle endurance and flexibility" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For the relaxation techniques the book's reflex rationale is in 7.2.1: prolonged resistance enhances "activation of the Golgi tendon reflex, thereby tending to reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and strong agonist contraction causes reciprocal "reflex relaxation of the antagonist muscles" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404, text layer). Siff does not tie each named technique to a specific reflex. Inference: CR and HR read as uses of the Golgi tendon mechanism and SRHR adds reciprocal inhibition through the final agonist contraction, but that pairing is this entry's reading.

**When to apply** — Use reversals (slow reversal, rhythmic stabilisation) when the target is coordination between opposing groups, and CR, HR or SRHR when the target is range under control rather than passive range. Siff's 7.5 extension: stretching would gain "markedly" if done "statically and dynamically over a full range with progressively increasing resistance incorporating relevant PNF procedures" instead of "in a static manner separately from the main exercises" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 56, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: warm-ups are where these partner techniques can be observed and dosed daily.

**When NOT to apply** — These are clinical techniques from Knott and Voss, described here without dosages, rest periods or outcome data; Siff gives none. CR and HR need a partner who can resist "as strongly as possible" and judge relaxation, so they do not scale to large groups without trained staff. Work stays inside "the limit of pain-free action" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), which matches principle 6, "Movement free of pain, but not free of effort" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Rhythmic Initiation is aimed at rigidity or spasticity, a patient problem, not a typical athlete one.

**Example** — Siff's procedure for CR, as he gives it: move the limb to its pain-free limit, have the client contract the antagonist dynamically while the practitioner resists maximally, command relaxation, wait for it, move the limb passively to its new limit, and repeat "gently for a few repetitions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). Inference: for a hamstring, the athlete lies supine with the leg raised to its limit and pushes the heel down against the partner's shoulder, relaxes, and the partner raises the leg further; the book does not name a muscle for this example.

For RC: "Repetition of muscle contraction is necessary for motor learning and the development of strength, muscle endurance and flexibility" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406). For the relaxation techniques the book's reflex rationale is in 7.2.1: prolonged resistance enhances "activation of the Golgi tendon reflex, thereby tending to reduce the tension in a muscle and promote local relaxation," and strong agonist contraction causes reciprocal "reflex relaxation of the antagonist muscles" (PDF p. 415 / printed p. 404, text layer). Siff does not tie each named technique to a specific reflex. Inference: CR and HR read as uses of the Golgi tendon mechanism and SRHR adds reciprocal inhibition through the final agonist contraction, but that pairing is this entry's reading.

# Novices Should Progress From Mobility to Stability, Following the Developmental Sequences PNF Is Built On

**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF methods "were formulated from findings on neuromuscular development, such as the functional evolution of all movement from motor immaturity to motor maturity in the growing child or novice athlete," progressing "total to individuated; proximal to distal, distal to proximal; mobile to stabile; gross to selective; reflexive to deliberate; overlapping to integrative; incoordinate to coordinate" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405, text layer). In 7.2.3.3 he restates the emphasis for "the patient, the novice or the child": "progression from primitive to complex, gross to individuated, mobile to stabile, reflexive to deliberative, proximal to distal, and incoordinate to coordinate." Then: "Contrary to common belief, the novice must be taught from a base of mobility to progress to stability, just as an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer).

**Why it works** — Siff's argument is the developmental analogy itself: the infant moves and staggers before standing stably (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He also states that "all physical conditioning requires a constant interplay of mobility and stability, all patterns implicate some parts of the body in stabilising and other parts in mobilising" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). He gives no training study for the novice-athlete claim.

**When to apply** — When teaching a beginner a new pattern, let them explore the movement through range before demanding rigid holds, and progress gross to selective and primitive to complex. Principle 21, "Planning of each phase to lay foundations for the next phase," and principle 20, "Progression from primitive to complex actions" (PDF p. 417 / printed p. 406), set the order. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the PNF sequence is one way to order those gradual exercise-selection steps for a freshman entering a lifting program.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an analogy from infant motor development extended to novice athletes, with no data in the book: confidence `untested`. The sequences are not one-directional. The 7.2.3 list gives both "proximal to distal, distal to proximal" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405), the novice paragraph gives "proximal to distal" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407), and principle 18 prescribes "distal to proximal sequences in neuromuscularly mature subjects" (PDF p. 416 / printed p. 405). Inference: read these as direction by maturity (proximal to distal while immature, distal to proximal once mature), but the book does not say this in one place. Siff names the "common belief" he opposes but does not cite who holds it. For a trained athlete, the goal can be the opposite: "the goal of training may be to prevent motion and to stimulate stability or maintain balance" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

**Example** — Siff's example is developmental, not athletic: "an infant learns to stand by first moving, staggering and exploring the environment" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). His athletic example of mixed demands: "both static strength and static muscular endurance might have to be developed in the back muscles of an athlete, while three-dimensional dynamic strength, dynamic muscular endurance and dynamic flexibility might have to be developed in the upper leg" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

# Rank Equipment by How Well It Allows Spiral-Diagonal Patterns: Pulleys and Dumbbells First, Barbells Next, Machines Last

**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) ranks equipment for modified PNF: "Pulleys and dumbbells are especially suitable for application of the spiral and diagonal, midline-crossing PNF techniques. ... Barbell training provides fewer opportunities for the use of PNF training, while machines offer the fewest possibilities of all" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image). Patterns are "Probably the most neglected aspect of PNF by coaches" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer). "No machines other than the traditional high-low pulley machines allow the user to produce PNF patterns," and "pec-decks, back hyperextension machines, seated pressing machines, hack-squat machines and leg extension machines ... cause such large deviations from recommended PNF patterns that they can impose excessive loading on certain joints and are suitable only for a small proportion of the training of highly conditioned athletes" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407, text layer). Machine training "requires a disproportionate number of machines to approximate the training offered by free weight and pulley training in three-dimensional space" (same page).

**Why it works** — Siff's reason is pattern fidelity: PNF patterns "stimulate more thorough involvement and motor development than the less-than-optimal patterns imposed by the abundance of linear or cam machines" (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407). Machine design "imposes body positions, postures and activation of pivots which usually differ considerably from those recommended by PNF and compromise the effectiveness and safety of the exercise" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). He calls the belief that machines offer "greater stability and safety for beginners than free weights" "A major error," and concludes "instructors must always 'spot' for the users of machines as well as free weights" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410).

**When to apply** — When choosing assistance exercises for rotational or overhead athletes, prefer cable and dumbbell versions that let the limb cross the midline and rotate. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: this heuristic applies inside that small assistance share; it does not argue for replacing the barbell core lifts.

**When NOT to apply** — Siff says it "does not imply that barbell and machine training should be avoided": they "can be used effectively under special circumstances, sometimes to cause intentional deviations from PNF patterns to adapt the body to potentially harmful actions which may occur in real sporting situations" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). No comparative data are given for the ranking or for the joint-loading claims about named machines. The "excessive loading" judgment on pec-decks and leg extensions is Siff's opinion in this passage. Inference: in rehab settings where Athletic Medicine wants a fixed path, a machine's constraint can be the point.

**Example** — Siff's examples: "The standing full-range cable cross-over exercise with external-internal rotation of the shoulder joint furnishes just one example of an adapted PNF pattern" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410); and in 7.5, for a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, cable-crossovers "in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern ... that cross the sagittal midline of the body" instead of the pec-deck (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Fig 7.8's caption adds that the trunk rotation pattern can be done supine or standing and "Resistance may be offered with a cable machine" (PDF p. 420 / printed p. 409, checked against the page image).

**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]] (4.2.7.1), [[heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use]] (4.2.7, the same "not safer than free weights" point), [[heuristic--equip-circuits-with-free-weights-and-pulleys-over-multistation-machines]], [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]

# Train for a Safety Factor Above Competition Forces, but Strength and Bulk Alone Do Not Protect an Inefficient Athlete

**What it is** — Under "Pattern Deviations and Safety Factors," Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) writes that PNF patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training, so that it is not incorrect to employ patterns of movement which may deviate significantly from those stipulated in PNF" (italics in the original). PNF keeps patterns "close to the body, a situation which occurs seldom in sport," where "forceful or rapid movements have to be executed with the distal extremities far from the relevant joints, thereby imposing large torque on these joints. If training always ensures that this degree of torque or force is avoided, then it will not prepare the athlete for the rigors of the sport and will increase susceptibility to overtraining and injury." Hence: "As in engineering, one must plan for a certain safety factor which allows the athlete to manage even larger forces than those which may be encountered in competition. For example, a safety factor of 1.2 means that a system can cope with a maximal loading of 0.2 or 20% greater than normally expected." Heavy supplementary resistance training ("cross training") serves this, "provided that it does not alter the neuromuscular patterns needed in the given sport." The limit: "Far too many athletes (e.g. in football and rugby) believe that increase in strength and bodymass will automatically protect them from injury. If one executes a movement in an inefficient manner or reacts too slowly to produce adequate force, then even gigantic strength or structural bulk can be inadequate to prevent injury." (All PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410, checked against the page image.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the engineering analogy and one sentence of reasoning: "high levels of skill and reactive ability in sport are vital in ensuring that sporting action is efficient and safe" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410). Inference: the claim has two parts, tissue capacity above expected load (the safety factor) and timing and skill to apply it (reactive ability), and the book makes both necessary and neither sufficient.

**When to apply** — When an exercise is rejected because it loads a joint at long lever arms, ask whether the sport imposes that torque; if it does, graded exposure is preparation, not risk. When a football player or coach treats added mass as injury armour, use the second half of the passage. # "Functional Training" Is Only a Synonym for Sport-Specific Training, and No Single Exercise Is "Non-Functional"

**What it is** — Siff (7.2 rests on his 1989 NSCA workshop, PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419) proposes replacing "modified PNF" with Functional Neuromuscular Conditioning (FNC), for five reasons: it is "sometimes desirable to deviate from strict PNF principles"; other disciplines ("Feldenkrais, Alexander, yoga, Tai Chi and Laban") add methods; contraction "may be facilitated by local after-discharge of the same muscle," so not all is neuromuscular; some PNF methods "may not be classified accurately as proprioceptive, such as cognitive, perceptual and other sensory mechanisms"; and the full name "is too technically daunting for the average coach or athlete." FNC "should be regarded as an entire conditioning system capable of developing any desired type of musculoskeletal fitness." He then turns to the fashion term: "Lately, the term 'functional training' has been promoted as a unique and modern method of training. In fact, it is nothing much more than a synonym for 'action specific', 'activity specific' or 'sport specific' training." To be accurate it "should address not only the motor qualities, but also the metabolic requirements of a given activity." And: "it is misleading to classify a single exercise as being "non-functional", since functional conditioning can comprise a combination of general and specific, 'functional' and 'non-functional' exercises. Indeed, this type of combined GPP and SPP methods forms the basis of all periodisation." (All PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image.)

**Why it works** — The argument is from programme level, not exercise level: function is a property of the whole combination of general (GPP) and specific (SPP) means over time, so labelling one exercise cannot settle it (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). Siff adds that "Because Wolff's Law states that function precedes structure, FNC may be seen to embrace all-round development of function and structure" (same page). Inference: Wolff's law is usually stated for bone remodelling under load; the book extends it here without further explanation.

**When to apply** — When a coach, vendor or athlete calls an exercise "functional" or "non-functional," ask which motor and metabolic demands of the sport it serves and where it sits in the GPP-to-SPP sequence. Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific."" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: Siff's point and the baseline agree; both replace a yes-or-no "functional" label with a position on a general-to-specific spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology argument with no data, so `untested`. It does not mean every exercise transfers equally: elsewhere the book sets strict criteria for transfer ([[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]) and warns that inappropriate resistance patterns "can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411). "Functional" here differs from the Chapter 1 sense of "functional" versus "structural" training ([[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]]), which is about neural versus hypertrophic effects, so check which meaning a source uses.

**Example** — Inference: a back squat is "non-functional" for a wide receiver only if judged alone; as a GPP means early in the off-season, followed by more specific acceleration and jump work, it is part of a functional programme in Siff's sense. The book gives no worked example for this section.

**Related** — [[framework--pnf-five-p-factors-and-principles-as-a-conditioning-system]], [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (a different use of "functional"), [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]], [[claim--core-stability-balance-training-has-no-shown-transfer-to-sport]] (7.4, Siff's other objection to "functional" fashions)

# Fradd (1995): Elbow Flexion Under Free Weight, Isokinetic and Combined Resistance

**What it is** — The authors report a study in which "the same group of subjects" did elbow flexion under free-weight (isoinertial), isokinetic, and combined resistance, the combination applied "using a cable machine specially designed and constructed for this purpose by one of Siff's mechanical engineering students at the University of the Witwatersrand in South Africa (Fradd, 1995)" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image). Number of subjects, their training status, loads and isokinetic speed are not given. Table 7.1 (velocity in m/s, power in W, force in N):

| Resistance | Max velocity | Mean power | Peak power | Mean force | Peak force |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Isoinertial | 1.49 | 151 | 306 | 184 | 219 |
| Isokinetic | 0.42 | 80 | 129 | 247 | 350 |
| Combined | 0.38 | 102 | 131 | 336 | 380 |

The five stated findings: (1) "Greatest mean and peak power is produced under free weight conditions, reaching a peak approximately midway through the movement"; (2) "Free weight force production is greatest during the earliest phases of joint movement"; (3) isokinetic and combined power is "considerably lower" but "remains near its peak value for a considerable part of the range"; (4) "Mean and peak force production is greatest during combined conditions, and may peak twice during the movement, most commonly near the beginning and the end of range"; (5) "Isokinetic force plateaus about one-third through the range, but commonly increases near end of range" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). For Fig 7.10 the text adds that peak power and velocity come "about halfway through the movement, when elbow angle is approximately 90 degrees," that "Approximately half the movement is spent in acceleration and half in deceleration," and that free-weight peak power is "some three times greater than under isokinetic or combined auxotonic-isokinetic conditions" (PDF p. 424 / printed p. 413, checked against the page image).

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for the differences beyond the resistance types themselves. They stress variability: curve shape "varies with every individual, according to their motor characteristics, and, in the combined scenario, with the magnitude of the inertial load and the velocity of isokinetic resistance"; combined resistance "may be made more auxotonic (free weight) if the added weight is large and more isokinetic if the added load is relatively small" (PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412). Inference: free weight lets the load accelerate and then forces deceleration, which yields high peak power mid-range; an isokinetic device caps velocity, so force can stay high while power stays low.

**When to apply** — When choosing a resistance mode for a goal: free weight for peak power, combined resistance for high force across the range. The authors' rule for all variable resistance: "it is important to fully understand the emphasis of the resistance training being used, because frequent use of any inappropriate training method or resistance pattern can be detrimental to the performance of the actual sporting movements," and for maximal power, "train regularly with loads that do not exceed about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411, checked against the page image). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — One single-joint movement, one unreported sample, a student project: confidence `untested`. Four places where the figures and the text do not match, read from the page images: (a) Table 7.1 gives 306 W against 129 and 131 W, about 2.4 times, while the text says "some three times greater" (PDF pp. 423-424). Inference: Figs 7.10-7.12 show peak power of about 350 against about 125-130 on the plotted scale, nearer three times, so the text may describe the figures rather than the table. (b) Fig 7.10's force curve starts at about 170 and peaks at about 230 near 20-40% of displacement, then declines slowly; the text says peak force is "near the beginning" (PDF p. 424). (c) Fig 7.12's combined force curve rises to about 350 by about 30%, holds, and is highest at about 85-90% before a sharp drop at the end; the double peak "near the beginning and the end of range" in finding 4 is not visible in this printed curve (PDF p. 424). (d) The 7.3 opening says greatest force is "usually ... possible after the joint has passed through the midpoint of the movement" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411), yet the free-weight data here put force highest early. Inference: the opening speaks of maximal joint strength across the range; Fig 7.10 shows force applied to a given accelerating load. Zatsiorsky describes ascending, descending and concave strength curves, with elbow flexion strongest at about 90 degrees ([[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--joint-strength-curves-sticking-points-and-moment-arm]]), so "after the midpoint" is not a general rule. Velocity and acceleration in Figs 7.10-7.12 share one unlabelled axis with force and power, so their plotted heights cannot be read as m/s.

**Example** — The study itself: in the combined condition, mean force was 336 N against 184 N under free weight, while peak power was 131 W against 306 W (Table 7.1, PDF p. 423 / printed p. 412, checked against the page image).

# Box Squat With Free Weights Plus Elastic Bands: Greater Force Through the Range and a Faster Descent

**What it is** — The authors describe a box squat in a power rack "with strong elastic bands attached between the ends of the bar and the base of the rack," band length set so resistance "varied between set limits at the lowest and the highest positions" (PDF pp. 424-425 / printed pp. 413-414, checked against the page images). The powerlifters (number not given) had "in addition to the squat weight of 200kg, an added elastic resistance of 150kg at the lowest position while sitting down on the box with knees at approximately right angles and a greatest elastic resistance of 250kg at the top of the squat with knees fully extended" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). The stated differences from free-weight training: "1. A greater mean and peak force were produced throughout the range of movement. 2. The descent onto the box tended to be accelerated above the normal gravitational rate of 9.8m/sec squared, so that greater eccentric force had to be generated to control the downward motion. 3. The stronger eccentric loading and the brief transition period involved while sitting before exploding upwards provided neuromuscular stimulation which approximates that usually encountered in popular plyometric training. 4. The force generated during the later stages increased, in strong contrast to the situation of normal squatting in which force production tends to decrease significantly" (PDF p. 425 / printed p. 414). # Four Forms of Accelerated Powermetrics: Raising Force by Acceleration Instead of Added Mass

**What it is** — The passage is written in the first person by one author ("Let me now elaborate," PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415). Inference: it sits in the Siff and Simmons context of 7.3 (Fig 7.9 and "The author has used ...", PDF p. 422) and is probably Siff's, but the page does not name him. Bands can "accelerate the load during the eccentric phase, thereby providing involuntary or passive acceleration," like plyometrics, where greater force in the amortisation phase comes from "momentum acting on the body through the acceleration of gravity (e.g., during a drop jump) or the action of a propelled object." There is also "an active or voluntary form ... which may be called actively accelerated powermetrics," usable in "the bench press, squat, dip for the jerk, 'Romanian deadlift' (or mid range clean pull from the hang)" and needing no partner or "plyometric bench" (PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415, checked against the page image). The four forms (same page):

1. Passively accelerated eccentrics with bands: "allow the elastic tension to accelerate the bar during this phase. Then, after a suitable range of movement, halt the movement as rapidly as you can."
2. Passively accelerated eccentrics with a partner, who pushes the bar down "like an inverse form of "forced reps"."
3. Actively accelerated eccentrics: "deliberately pull the bar downwards as fast as you can and stop the downward motion before you reach the end of the movement." Unlike bands, "the force added to gravitational force ceases if one stops voluntarily accelerating the bar."
4. Actively accelerated ballistics (rebounds): pull down as fast as possible, stop "at a suitable point before the end of the movement and as rapidly as you can, try to accelerate the bar upwards into a powerful concentric movement."

**Why it works** — The stated principle: "this form of training, according to Newton's Second Law, focuses on force being increased by means of acceleration and not added mass" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416, checked against the page image). The author calls it "really a type of 'supramaximal' force training" (same page). No measurements of the forces produced are given.

**When to apply** — When an athlete needs higher eccentric and amortisation forces than the bar weight alone supplies, without heavier loads or drop equipment. Start "with relatively light loads in the bench press or squat (say, about 40-50kg, depending on your strength and training experience) and use very few repetitions," with "considerably lower" loads for smaller muscle groups (PDF pp. 426-427 / printed pp. 415-416). Load ceiling: "maximal power production, depending on the specific exercise, occurs with loads of between 50-70 percent of one's 1RM, so it is unnecessary ever to exceed this range of loading in these accelerated training methods (unless one uses them over a very small range of motion)" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides)). Inference: these are advanced options for that already-strong group, not for athletes still building relative strength.

**When NOT to apply** — The author warns: "do not overestimate your capabilities, because all of these forms of accelerated powermetrics can be very demanding on the body," and they "can impose extremely large stresses on your soft tissues" (PDF pp. 426-427 / printed pp. 415-416). For safety "do not allow the accelerated load to force you into your extreme end position of joint action" (PDF p. 426). No training study, injury data or force data are given: confidence `untested`. The book gives two power-load ranges six pages apart: "about 60-70 percent of one's maximum" (PDF p. 422 / printed p. 411) and "between 50-70 percent of one's 1RM" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Both differ from the Chapter 3 figures of about 25% of maximal force in isotonic laboratory models and about two-thirds of maximum in the competition squat ([[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]]); Jandacka and Vaverka 2008 put the acceleration-phase optimum at 47-63% 1RM by sex and exercise in untrained students (vault brief, p. 11). Inference: treat 50-70% as a broad zone, not a fixed number.

**Example** — The author's own starting point: an accelerated-eccentric bench press or squat with "about 40-50kg" and very few repetitions (PDF p. 426 / printed p. 415). Inference: an actively accelerated ballistic bench at that load would be pulled down fast, stopped a few centimetres above the chest, and driven up at once.

**Related** — [[case-study--box-squat-with-free-weights-plus-elastic-bands]] (band-accelerated descent), [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]], [[claim--maximal-power-output-load-differs-lab-vs-competition-lift]], [[research-papers/jandacka-2008-a-regression-model-to-determine-load-for-maximum-power-output]], [[research-papers/handford-2024-a-conceptual-framework-of-different-eccentric-training-methods]] (maps accelerated eccentric loading among eccentric methods), [[framework--compensatory-acceleration-training]]

2. Passively accelerated eccentrics with a partner, who pushes the bar down "like an inverse form of "forced reps"."
3. Actively accelerated eccentrics: "deliberately pull the bar downwards as fast as you can and stop the downward motion before you reach the end of the movement." Unlike bands, "the force added to gravitational force ceases if one stops voluntarily accelerating the bar."

# Core Stabilisation on Balls and Boards, and Cueing the Transversus Abdominis, Have No Shown Transfer to Sport

**What it is** — The authors write that, "largely as a consequence of individuals attempting to extrapolate to the general fitness world some of the muscle isolating methods used by physical therapists for injury rehabilitation, it has become fairly fashionable to encounter special programmes to train 'core stabilisation' with balancing tools such as wobble boards and physio balls, augmented by activation of the transversus abdominis (TA) to strengthen the trunk." Three objections follow. First, "stability of the core or trunk cannot be exhibited without the periphery of the body being firmly secured on a solid surface, unless, of course, the athlete has to use the core independently of the floor or any other apparatus, as in diving, trampolining and jumping." Second, "Well meaning instructions to activate TA during dynamic actions such as lifting and wrestling are highly inappropriate, because conscious intervention in any such movements can lead to "paralysis by analysis"," and "if the athlete is taught the optimal way to carry out any movement, the body naturally activates muscles in the most appropriate way for that given activity. After all, the body "knows only of movement, not muscles"." Third, "no research has yet shown that isolationist training or ball/board balancing skills transpose to 'functional' sporting action, so that time spent on such pursuits usually can be better spent on more sport specific drills, unless the aim is to resolve some injury." (All PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416, checked against the page image.)

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning rests on two earlier points in the same section: isolation is load-dependent, "Isolation may occur to a significant extent when the resistance to movement is small, but with increasing load, the relevant stabilisers of the body and joints, as well as assistant movers, come more strongly into play," and "all human movement involves the intricate orchestration of concurrent and sequential contractions of movers and stabilisers" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Inference: if stabilisers are recruited by the task and load, a well-learned loaded movement already trains them, and a separate isolation drill adds little; the book states the premises, not this full chain.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's programme spends time on unstable-surface or TA-isolation drills, ask whether that time would be better spent on loaded, sport-specific work, and keep coaching cues external to the movement rather than to a single muscle. The exception the authors grant is rehabilitation: "unless the aim is to resolve some injury" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416), which in Baylor terms is Athletic Medicine's call. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints); single-joint assistance work is kept to a small share of total volume." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104, Inferred (transcript + slides)).

**When NOT to apply** — "No research has yet shown" is a statement about the evidence when the book was written, with no citation, and the book gives no study of its own: confidence `untested`. No entry in the vault or staging library covers core stability or unstable-surface training, so the claim could not be checked against another library source. The authors themselves exempt sports where the core works without a fixed base ("diving, trampolining and jumping") and injury rehabilitation. "Paralysis by analysis" is asserted, not measured.

**Example** — The authors' own: instructing a lifter or wrestler to brace the transversus abdominis during the action, which they call "highly inappropriate" (PDF p. 427 / printed p. 416). Inference: a coach would instead teach the squat or the takedown well and let trunk activation follow the task.

**Related** — [[claim--muscle-isolation-is-load-dependent-mostly-illusory-under-heavy-load]] (4.2.9, cited by the authors as the earlier discussion), [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] (the "Limitations of Anatomical Movement Analysis" section 7.4 asks the reader to bear in mind), [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[claim--trunk-rotation-is-driven-by-the-obliques-not-the-erector-spinae]]

# Do Heel Raises With Inversion to Load All Plantarflexors, and Train Dorsiflexion With Both Inversion and Eversion

**What it is** — The authors: "so-called 'calf raises' or 'heel raises' are commonly regarded as exercises to develop gastrocnemius and soleus. However, it should be noted that plantarflexion also involves action of plantaris, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis posterior. Moreover, inward rotation or inversion of the foot more strongly recruits the last three muscles named, so that heel raises with inversion tend to activate all of the plantarflexors more strongly." And: "Popular emphasis on heel raising invariably causes one to neglect the antagonistic action of the dorsiflexors such as tibialis anterior. The summary above reveals that it is important to dorsiflex with both inversion and eversion of the ankle if all dorsiflexors are to be exercised adequately." (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418, checked against the page image; the text has a stray "in" in "heel raising in invariably".) The 7.4.1 summary it rests on lists dorsiflexion as "Tibialis anterior, peroneus tertius, extensor hallucis longus, and extensor digitorum longus," inversion as "Flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior, assisted by extensor hallucis longus," and eversion as "Extensor digitorum longus, peroneus tertius, peroneus longus, peroneus brevis" (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418).

**Why it works** — The reasoning is the joint-action summary itself: each dorsiflexor also inverts (tibialis anterior) or everts (peroneus tertius, extensor digitorum longus), so one straight dorsiflexion pattern under-loads one side, and the deep plantarflexors that also invert are loaded more when inversion is added (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). No EMG data are given. Inference: confidence `supported` rests on the joint actions being standard functional anatomy, not on any outcome data for the training advice.

**When to apply** — Programming calf and shin work for running, jumping and cutting athletes, or when an athlete's lower-leg work is heel raises only. Eric's baseline: "The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 78, Inferred (protocol)). Inference: that test loads plantarflexion in a neutral foot position; the authors' point suggests the training side should also include inverted heel raises and dorsiflexion in both directions, while the test stays standardised.

**When NOT to apply** — The two lists do not fully agree, as printed. The 7.4.2 passage names tibialis posterior among the muscles that inversion "more strongly recruits," but the 7.4.1 inversion list does not include tibialis posterior, and the 7.4.1 plantarflexion list does not include flexor hallucis longus, which 7.4.2 names as a plantarflexor (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: standard anatomy lists tibialis posterior as an invertor, so the 7.4.1 list looks incomplete rather than the 7.4.2 claim wrong, but the book does not resolve it. This is advice for assistance work; it does not replace the loading of gastrocnemius and soleus that sprinting and jumping demand ([[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]]). Loaded inversion is not a choice for an athlete with an acute lateral ankle sprain without Athletic Medicine's direction.

**Example** — The authors' own example is the heel raise and its neglected antagonist, tibialis anterior (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: a weekly lower-leg block could pair standing heel raises with the foot turned in with banded dorsiflexion done once toward inversion and once toward eversion.

# Twenty-Two Observations Any Hypertrophy Formula Must Satisfy

**What it is** — The authors argue that "Any Hypertrophy Formula has to be based on many well-known observations on muscle physiology and mechanics," and that the target is really "musculo-collagenous hypertrophy, since training affects the entire muscle complex, not just the muscles" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). They list 22 observations (PDF pp. 430-431 / printed pp. 419-420, checked against the page images). Inference: the six groups below are this entry's grouping; the wording inside quotes is theirs.

- Stimulus and limit: "The fundamental stimulus in all strength and tissue hypertrophy quite simply is physical loading" (1), which "must not exceed the mechanical strength of the tissues involved" (2); growth can also be stimulated by "active muscle contraction, passive stretching, vibrational oscillation or external electrical stimulation" (22).
- Threshold and overload: increase "is minimal unless a certain minimal threshold load is imposed" (5); "The minimal threshold is not fixed, but increases with level of adaptation, which ensures that rate of progress slows down or ceases" (6); continued increase needs "progressive incremental increase in loading" (10).
- Timing: gains occur "predominantly during a certain recovery period after loading" (3); they are "not linear or continuous. For example, a 10% increase in load does not necessarily produce a 10% increase in strength" (11); they "diminish if physical loading is not imposed regularly" (21).
- Tissue differences: "All tissues do not hypertrophy or strengthen at the same rate or to the same degree" (4); fibre groups differ in fatigue and force (18); "Increase in strength is not necessarily associated with increase in hypertrophy or vice versa" (20).
- How tension is made: effects depend on "the way in which the tension is produced or maintained," for example "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (8); tension "varies between zero and a certain maximum as joint angles change" (16) and across concentric, eccentric and isometric modes (17).
- Nervous system and fatigue: "Muscles rarely are able to produce 100% of their maximum potential" because of protective reflex inhibition (12); gains "may or may not be associated with some form of fatigue" (13); fatigue limits and reflex inhibition are hard to tell apart (14); fatigue is "multi-faceted" (15); and gains "ultimately are the result of specific patterns of nervous excitation" (19).

Their conclusion: these "should suffice to show that a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

**Why it works** — The list works as a set of constraints: any single-variable rule (one tempo, one rep count, one tension time) will violate several observations at once, such as the rising threshold (6), non-linearity (11) and the different ways tension can be produced (8) (PDF pp. 430-431). The authors cite no studies for the 22 items and call them "well-known observations."

**When to apply** — When judging a hypertrophy prescription or a coach's formula, test it against the list: does it overload above a threshold that rises, allow recovery, vary how tension is made, and accept that size and strength can move separately? Eric's baseline: "The preparatory period is sequenced hypertrophy/work-capacity, then basic strength, then strength-to-power, each with defined intensity/volume bands (e.g., hypertrophy phase 50-75% intensity, 3-6 sets of 5-20 reps; strength phase 80-90% intensity, moderate volume)" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 180, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the band approach fits the authors' view better than a single formula, since it sets ranges rather than one prescriptive number.

**When NOT to apply** — The list is uncited, so `supported` rests on most items matching established training physiology (the threshold and overload items agree with [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]] and item 4 with [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]]), not on evidence given here. It is a set of constraints, not a prescription: it gives no loads, sets, reps or frequencies. Item 22's passive stretching, vibration and electrical stimulation are listed without doses or comparisons. The section is aimed at bodybuilders and physique work, not at athletes whose priority is performance.

**Example** — The authors' item 8 example: tension can be raised either with "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load (in accordance with Newton II: Force = Mass x Acceleration)" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

**Related** — [[claim--time-under-tension-alone-does-not-determine-hypertrophy]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]], [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]], [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (1.13, the authors' two types of hypertrophy), [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] (strength and size as separate training effects)

# Time Under Tension Alone Does Not Determine Hypertrophy: Tension Must Exceed a Threshold, and How It Is Produced Matters

**What it is** — The authors take on one formula: "every exercise must maintain a prolonged muscle tension time for at least 40 seconds or so if one wishes to produce maximal hypertrophy" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Their counter-claims: "The concept of tension time per se is meaningless, since loading even for very prolonged periods may have no effects of strength and hypertrophy if the tension does not exceed this minimum threshold" (item 7); "The effects of tension on tissue depend not only on the magnitude or duration of the tension, but the way in which the tension is produced or maintained" (item 8); and "Long periods of muscle 'time under tension' as imposed by cyclical activities such as endurance running, cycling and swimming are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (item 9) (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420, checked against the page image). They conclude that "a 'Time Under Tension' formula or any other highly prescriptive rule is oversimplistic" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is the threshold: if tension is below the minimum that triggers adaptation (item 5), adding time does not help (item 7), and endurance sports are their natural experiment of long tension time without growth (item 9) (PDF pp. 430-431). They also note tension can be raised by acceleration as well as mass, "a large, slowly accelerated load or a smaller, rapidly accelerated load" (item 8), so a slow tempo is not the only route to high tension.

**When to apply** — When an athlete or coach prescribes slow tempos to hit a fixed tension time, check first that the load is heavy enough to matter, and do not slow the bar at the cost of intent in athletes whose goal is power. Eric's baseline: "Tracy Fober's maxim ("use a barbell like a chisel, not a sledgehammer") is adopted as a guiding standard: prioritize movement quality and confidence-through-competence over chasing hypertrophy or 1RM numbers, especially early in a training cycle." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 109, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the authors' point supports that stance, since no single number, tension time included, should drive the programme.

**When NOT to apply** — The section cites no hypertrophy studies; `supported` rests on the threshold argument and item 9's endurance-sport observation, not on trials comparing tempos. Two voices need separating. The opening quotes are from unnamed commentators, not the authors: "All the big bodybuilders who I trained with did their reps pretty fast, which makes me seriously question the Time Under Tension theory" and "People with extreme genetics who are using huge amounts of drugs will probably get big no matter what kind of weight training and rep speed they're doing. What's more important is finding out how much rep speed matters for a natural bodybuilder with average genetics" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419). The authors endorse only the second, saying its author "is probably far closer to the truth than anyone who religiously propounds simplistic Tension Time theories" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420). The closing paragraph on marketing and the public's taste for "cerebrally undemanding mantras" (PDF p. 431) is opinion with no evidence. The claim does not say tension time is irrelevant, only that it is not sufficient on its own.

**Example** — The authors' own: endurance running, cycling and swimming impose long "time under tension" but "are not known generally to produce significant increases in strength or hypertrophy" (PDF p. 431 / printed p. 420).

The patterns "were devised for rehabilitation, not elite sporting training" (PDF p. 421 / printed p. 410), so strict PNF is not the goal for athletes (see [[principle--train-for-a-safety-factor-above-competition-forces]]). Inference: Starling's law is usually stated for cardiac muscle; the book gives no explanation of the link. Classical PNF is hands-on clinical work; Siff points coaches to the NSCA videotapes (Siff, 1989) rather than describing every technique (PDF p. 418 / printed p. 407).

-**Example** — Siff's own: for a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "he would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").

+**Example** — From 7.5: a coach applying the 7.2 list to a baseball pitcher or javelin thrower, instead of the pec-deck, "would recommend the use of a pulley machine in a specific spiral-diagonal pattern (see 7.2.3.1) of cable-crossovers that cross the sagittal midline of the body," performed "over a comfortable full range," involving "multiple joints besides just the shoulder" with joints positioned "to optimise strengthening" (PDF p. 430 / printed p. 419, checked against the page image). Figs 7.3-7.8 (PDF pp. 419-420 / printed pp. 408-409, checked against the page images) draw the upper-extremity, lower-extremity and trunk patterns, each labelled with its three component motions (for example "Flexion to Extension, Abduction to Adduction, Ext to Int Rotation").

**Related** — [[framework--pnf-activation-and-relaxation-techniques]], [[claim--novices-progress-from-mobility-to-stability-pnf-sequence]], [[heuristic--use-pulleys-and-dumbbells-for-spiral-diagonal-pnf-patterns]], [[claim--functional-training-means-sport-specific-and-no-exercise-is-non-functional]], [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]] (the reflexes PNF uses, Fig 3.33), [[claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance]] (the overflow principle), [[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]] (PNF as a stretching category, 3.5.8), [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]] (PNF use of the positive supportive reaction)

**When to apply** — Programming calf and shin work for running, jumping and cutting athletes, or when an athlete's lower-leg work is heel raises only. Eric's baseline: "The isometric seated calf raise is run on the ForceDecks "Mid-Thigh Pull" setting: 90-degree ankle/knee position, belt pre-tensioned to a fingertip's gap, 3 maximal 6-second contractions with 15 seconds' rest between reps." (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 78, Inferred (protocol)). Inference: that test loads plantarflexion in a neutral foot position; the authors' point suggests the training side should also include inverted heel raises and dorsiflexion in both directions, while the test stays standardised.

-**When NOT to apply** — The two lists do not fully agree, as printed. The 7.4.2 passage names tibialis posterior among the muscles that inversion "more strongly recruits," but the 7.4.1 inversion list does not include tibialis posterior, and the 7.4.1 plantarflexion list does not include flexor hallucis longus, which 7.4.2 names as a plantarflexor (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: standard anatomy lists tibialis posterior as an invertor, so the 7.4.1 list looks incomplete rather than the 7.4.2 claim wrong, but the book does not resolve it. This is advice for assistance work; it does not replace the loading of gastrocnemius and soleus that sprinting and jumping demand ([[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]]). Loaded inversion is not a choice for an athlete with an acute lateral ankle sprain without Athletic Medicine's direction.

+**When NOT to apply** — The two lists do not fully agree, as printed. The 7.4.2 passage names tibialis posterior among the muscles that inversion "more strongly recruits," but the 7.4.1 inversion list does not include tibialis posterior, and the 7.4.1 plantarflexion list does not include flexor hallucis longus, which 7.4.2 names as a plantarflexor (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: check the tibialis posterior omission against an anatomy reference before teaching the 7.4.1 list as complete; the book does not resolve it. This is advice for assistance work; it does not replace the loading of gastrocnemius and soleus that sprinting and jumping demand ([[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--ankle-plantar-flexors-as-main-sprint-driver]]). Loaded inversion is not a choice for an athlete with an acute lateral ankle sprain without Athletic Medicine's direction.

**Example** — The authors' own example is the heel raise and its neglected antagonist, tibialis anterior (PDF p. 429 / printed p. 418). Inference: a weekly lower-leg block could pair standing heel raises with the foot turned in with banded dorsiflexion done once toward inversion and once toward eversion.

I finished batch 7b with 14 new entries, which completes Chapter 7 at PDF 431. Lint is clean on all 14 files. I added files only: no existing entry or `_book.md` was edited, I made no vault edits and ran no git.

**Entries by kind and confidence**
- Framework, 5: three `supported` (PNF five P-factors, PNF activation and relaxation techniques, hypertrophy observations) and two `untested` (accelerated powermetrics, which are written up only for the bench press and squat).
- Claim, 5: two `supported` (trunk rotation from the obliques, time under tension) and three `untested` (novices progress from mobility to stability, "functional training" means sport-specific, core stability training).
- Heuristic, 2: one `supported` (heel raises with inversion) and one `untested` (pulleys and dumbbells for PNF patterns).
- Principle, 1, `untested`: train for a safety factor above competition forces.
- Case study, 2: the Fradd 1995 elbow-flexion study is `untested`. The box squat with bands is `contested`, because Frost 2010 (review p. 21) says transfer to sport was not demonstrated and most acute studies found no difference from load-matched free weights. Rhea 2009 points the other way, and the entry records both.

**Entry count per section (for `_book.md`)**

| Section | Printed pp | PDF idx | Entries |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.2 PNF (7.2.1-7.2.5) | 403-411 | 414-422 | 6 (PDF 419-420 are figure-only) |
| 7.3 Combinations of Resistance Methods | 411-416 | 422-427 | 3 |
| 7.4 Muscle Training (7.4.1-7.4.2) | 416-418 | 427-429 | 3 |
| 7.5 Use of Strength Training Compendium | 418-419 | 429-430 | 0 on its own; its pec-deck vs cable-crossover example and stretching point are folded into the PNF framework, pulley heuristic and techniques entries |
| 7.6 Training for Hypertrophy? | 419-420 | 430-431 | 2 |

The 7.4.1 joint-movement list and the 7.5 compendium list were not atomized, as instructed.

**Where I stopped:** at the end of Chapter 7, PDF 431. Chapter 8 starts at PDF 432 / printed 421. The top of PDF 414 (items 13-28 and "Concluding Remarks") belongs to 7.1, so I left it to the other atomizer. Section 7.2 starts mid-page on PDF 414.

**Voice**
- **7.2 is Siff's.** PDF 430 / printed 419 says his 1989 NSCA workshop "acted as the basis for Chapter 7.2," and PDF 429 says "the author was invited ... (Siff, 1989)".
- **7.3 is mixed.** PDF 422 has "The author has used" next to the Siff and Simmons photo. PDF 423 refers to "one of Siff's ... students" in the third person, so I wrote that passage as the authors'. The powermetrics passage is first person ("Let me", PDF 426); I marked it as probably Siff but not named on the page.
- **7.6 quotes unnamed commentators.** I labelled their words as quotes, not as the authors' statements.

**Unclear or contradictory spots** (all recorded in the entries with their pages)
- **Power-load range:** "about 60-70 percent" (PDF 422 / printed 411) against "50-70 percent of one's 1RM" (PDF 427 / printed 416).
- **Table 7.1 against the text:** peak power is 306 W against 129 and 131 W, about 2.4 times. The text says "some three times greater" (PDF 423-424).
- **Fig 7.10 against the text:** free-weight force peaks at about 20-40% of the movement, but the text says "near the beginning".
- **Fig 7.12:** the double force peak described in the text is not visible in the printed curve.
- **7.3 opening against the data:** the opening says greatest force comes "after the joint has passed through the midpoint". The study's own free-weight data put force highest early, and Zatsiorsky describes three strength-curve shapes.
- **Proximal and distal sequences:** PDF 416 gives both directions, principle 18 says distal to proximal for mature subjects, and PDF 418 says proximal to distal for novices.
- **Other source oddities:** "Starling's Law" is used for the stretch reflex (PDF 417); "brachialis and brachialis" appears on PDF 427.
- **Ankle lists:** 7.4.1's inversion list leaves out tibialis posterior, but 7.4.2 names it; flexor hallucis longus is missing from the plantarflexion list (PDF 429).
- **Uncited claims:** that multifidus is "the only" back rotator (PDF 429), and the extension of Wolff's law to "functional training" (PDF 422).
- **No library source to check against:** nothing in the vault or staging covers core stability, so that claim stays `untested`.

- I rendered PDF 414-418 but did not open them; quotes from those pages are text-layer only, and the entries say so.

- Figs 7.10-7.12 plot all curves on one unlabelled axis, so velocity and acceleration heights cannot be read as real values.

- `heuristic--nfr-machine-limitations-safety-and-appropriate-use`, `framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines` and the equip-circuits heuristic → the pulley heuristic.

- Jandacka 2008, Handford 2024 and the 3.3.2 power-load claim → powermetrics.
- Bompa's progressive-overload threshold, the differential-tissue claim and the sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic framework → the two hypertrophy entries.
- Moyer's plantar-flexor claim → the heel-raise heuristic.
